Analysis
The story is an example of what David Stubbs calls "neo-traditional" literature, in which contemporary Inuit deal with the challenges of modern life while retaining their traditional culture. In this story, the challenge is the incompatibility of traditional and modern ways of life, and the decision the inexperienced man must make between them. The story also demonstrates the importance of experience and the dangers of ignorance. The two men represent the positive and negative aspects of the Inuit way of life, and the story is a cautionary tale about the dangers of forgetting traditional knowledge.

Background
This painting was done in 1970 by George Beaverhouse, a member of the Egulac band of Cree. It is based on a true story that happened in 1959. This painting is one of the most famous works of Native American art. It has been reproduced many times. Beaverhouse himself has made many reproductions of this painting. He would often add new elements to the painting, such as airplanes.

After several days, the whites were allowed to trade, and left the camp. The incident is recounted in "The Ballad of Patch Adams", the song that gives the film of the same name its title.

The apparition is that of the two men, although sometimes only one of them is seen. They are seen sitting quietly, facing the fire, with an air of sadness on their faces. Sometimes, they will disappear suddenly, leaving behind only the smell of wood smoke. Other times, they will be seen for days on end, sitting silently, never saying anything.

History
Many years later, I was sitting with my friend Jack Fuselier, reminiscing about the old days, when I suddenly saw the two men sitting across the fire from us. I nudged Jack and whispered, "Do you see them?" He nodded, and we sat in silence, watching them for a long time. Finally, they disappeared, leaving us in wonder.

This story was told to me by "Old Man" Rosalie La Lone, who said that it was told to him by his father, who was a trapper in the area where the Egulac people were camped.

The story is a common theme in many Eskimo tales.  It was recorded by Peter Freuchen in 1914 when he was visiting the missions in Egulac.

Analysis
This story is an example of the Eskimo taboo against wasting food.  In this story, the two men from Egulac did not kill the two Europeans, but left them to die of exposure, thereby wasting their bodies.  According to Marston, this is an exception to the general Eskimo rule that it is proper to kill even enemies who are starving or about to die of exposure, in order to save their bodies for later use.  Marston relates another story in which this same Egulac group killed a seal they had trapped, but did not eat the meat, in order to save it for a future feast.

The basic theme is that a person or group of persons is trapped on the ice, which then gives way and causes them to fall into the water, usually with disastrous results.

The people of Egulac were divided into three groups: those who killed Mikiuk, those who knew who killed Mikiuk and those who did nothing. The man who was responsible for bringing Mikiuk's body back to the village was punished by having to pull the sled with Mikiuk's body on it for a distance of 16 kilometres (9.9 mi). He was also forbidden to hunt for one year.

The answer is: a native tribe from British Columbia, Canada, were walking home from a drinking party in December 1916 when they were assaulted by four white men. One of the natives, named Frank, was shot and killed, the other, named Joe, was taken to the home of a white man named Johnson. Johnson's brother, George, and friend, Alex Machette, had been in an argument earlier in the evening and were intoxicated. When the two men noticed the Egulac men, they lured them into their home and beat them with a variety of weapons, including a rifle, a shotgun, a club, and their fists. The Egulac men were beaten so severely that they were left for dead. The following morning, Johnson and Machette brought the badly injured Joe to a hospital in New Westminster, British Columbia. Joe died two days later, on December 18, 1916.
The case was heard by the Supreme Court of British Columbia in May 1917. The judge found the defendants (Johnson and Machette) guilty of assault and ordered them to pay a fine of $200, plus the cost of the Egulac man's burial. The court noted that while the Egulac men were drunk, they were still entitled to the same protection under the law as any other man. The judge admonished the police for not arresting the Egulac men when they were first beaten, saying that an attempt should be made to keep natives and whites separate when intoxicated.The incident was one of a series of events that led to the passage of the Indian Act in 1917, which gave the Canadian government greater control over the internal affairs of native communities.

Adaptation
In 1933, a French journalist by the name of Anatole Boutrousse visited the village of Egulac. A native of the village, Pierre Scherbatcheff (or Scherbatcheff-Zerektive), told Boutrousse the story of the two men who fell through the ice. Boutrousse adapted the story for French audiences, adding in the character of the village elder and changing the ending to make it clear that the speaker was the culprit. The story was published in the January 1934 issue of the magazine Combat and was later collected in book form as Les Cités Obscures (1937). The story was translated into English in 1940 as "The Men of Egulac".

History
This event took place in 1871 along the banks of the Fraser River, in what is now British Columbia. The two men were named Nootka and Wovoka. They were from the Egulac tribe of the Wakashan linguistic stock. They were peaceful and unarmed, gathering berries and other plant foods. When the Indians moved into their camp, the whites moved out. For this reason, the whites got the name "Ghost Indians" from the Indians' habit of appearing and disappearing.

Significance
This event illustrates a common theme in the relations between Native Americans and white people. The whites assumed that all Native Americans were hostile and wanted to attack them. This caused many unnecessary conflicts between the two groups.

He was intoxicated and would only trade his furs for liquor. The other man, named Piasati, was sober and knew the Egulac had a strict code of conduct. According to Cree tradition, intoxication was no excuse for breaking the code. Piasati therefore fought Okabe. He tied him to a pole and left him for three days. When he returned, Okabe was dead. Piasati therefore had to kill himself, as according to the code, a man who kills another must die. They saw the two men buried in the ground, with a cross on Okabe's side and a pole on Piasati's side. They knew the story of what had happened, and they approved of Piasati's actions. However, they also felt that Okabe's burial was not proper for a married man. They therefore dug up Okabe's body and buried it properly.

The answer is: (a fictional Inuit community) were travelling from one camp to another on the great ice plain of Labrador. One was experienced and skilled in navigating by stars, the other was not. They had decided to travel by night, using the moon to guide them. The experienced navigator, whose camp it was, took the lead. He tied the two men together by a long line and off they set. The inexperienced man soon became frightened. He did not trust the guide and began to pull back on the line. This went on for some time, until the guide told the other to stop. He then took a knife and cut the line. The two men fell to the ice, but the guide pulled the inexperienced man to safety. He then took a gun and shot the other man, thus leaving him to die of exposure.

History
This story is a variant of an older Inuit story, and was collected by Richard Harpoe, a teacher in the mission at Egulac. It was recorded in 1924, though the events it describes may have taken place many years earlier.
It is told as an example of the consequences of fear and mistrust in the book Eskimo Stories, published in 1925, by Frank Speck and Richard Finch Harpoe. The book was reprinted in 1961 by the Department of Education for the Government of the Northwest Territories, with an introduction by John C. Ough.

Analysis
The story is an example of a type of Inuit story known as "traditional stories", or more specifically, "teaching stories". These stories were used by elders to teach children (and sometimes adults) about the ways of the world, and often feature animals or supernatural beings. This story, for example, teaches listeners not to let fear and mistrust rule their actions.

The tale
The tale of "One Night Two Men" is a common one in Inuit folklore. It is told to explain why the Inuit do not travel on the ice at night. Another reason why this taboo exists is that, due to the refraction of light through the ice, objects on the surface of the frozen water appear distorted and unfamiliar, making it difficult for a person to distinguish between safe paths and dangerous cracks in the ice.

Variants
Similar tales are told by other Arctic peoples. For example, among the Yupik people of Alaska, a similar story is told of two men named Allak and Chukko, who were pursued by a sea monster called Kuvlak.

This story is told by the protagonist of "The Edge of the Earth", a novel by Michael McGhee, who hears it from an old Inuit man on the frozen shore of the fjord.It is an example of a type of story that is told in many Indigenous communities, and is often called a "noisy story" or "story with a noise". It is called this because when the story is told, the listener is asked to make a noise at certain points, usually when a sudden action occurs in the story. For example, when the man fell through the ice, the listener would make a sound like the ice cracking. When the storyteller comes to the end of the story and says "That's all", the listener makes a noise to show that the story has ended.

The Egulac tribe is one of several groups of Native Americans who were displaced by the fur trade in Canada. In the early 19th century, the Egulac lived along the shores of Hudson Bay near what is now York Factory. When the Hudson's Bay Company established a trading post there, the Egulac were forced to move south. They eventually settled along the banks of the Churchill River near what is now Churchill Island (50°N 102°W), which was named after them. When the buffalo disappeared, the Egulac were forced to depend on the whites for trade goods. Background
The story is a part of the oral tradition of the Inuit. It was recorded by Donald Fraser Healey in 1978 while he was working as a social worker in the Northwest Territories. Analysis
Inuit stories often involve hunting and the natural world. This story is no exception. The two men are traveling across the frozen lake, presumably to visit another Inuit camp. They come across a polar bear and both men take part in the hunt. After the hunt, the men cut up the bear and store the meat for later use. The men then continue on their journey. The story does not specify whether the men reached their destination or encountered any other events on their journey.

Context
This is the first part of the story "One Night Two Men" by Richard Grouse (1913–1991), a white man who spent several decades living among the people of the Egulac tribe in northern British Columbia. The men were named Patsy and Frank.The story is told from the perspective of "Mr. Smith", the protagonist of several other Grouse stories. It was recorded by Grouse's friend and biographer, Tom Mowat. Mowat wrote down Grouse's stories in the 1970s, a few years after Grouse died.

Analysis
The story is an example of the literary style of "tedious narrative" described by North American ethnologist Francis Healey in his 1912 article "Narrative Types", in which a great deal of information is conveyed in a seemingly trivial or inconsequential manner.In this story, the Egulac men are presented as being almost inhuman in their greed and their inability to satisfy their desires for food. Their requests for more food are not accompanied by any indication of when or how they will satisfy their demands. The implication is that they will continue to ask for food until they are given all of the food in the camp. The story does not go on to describe any consequences of this incident. It simply ends with the Egulac men asking for more.

It was told to him by an elder of the community, who asked that it not be recorded until after his death. Finch agreed to this, and did not publish the story until after the man's death in 1968. Even then, he did not attribute the story to its actual teller, calling it instead "an Egulac story".

Adaptations
In 1971, the CBC broadcast a children's series called The Adventures of Uncle Nick, based on Finch's stories. The story of "One Night Two Men" was adapted for the series' third episode, "The Murdered Man". Finch himself wrote the script for this episode.
